outcome: Since 26 January 2024 the general bounds on the Borsuk number are unchanged, but the per-dimension record has moved in three places: a 63-dimensional counterexample was posted in May 2026 (Grinsztajn, with GPT-5.5 Pro, and separately by Ji with ChatGPT GPT-5.6 Sol, the latter withdrawn in August 2026); an upper bound of 8 for dimension 4 was posted in May 2026 (Tolmachev and Voronov, computer search); and on 6 October 2026 OpenAI released a Lean-formalised claim that a nine-dimensional set cannot be covered by ten pieces of smaller diameter, which would lower the smallest known failing dimension from 63 to 9, with no public expert check yet found.
problem_asks: Read from the statement alone. (a) Let f(n) be the least number of pieces of strictly smaller diameter into which every bounded set of diameter 1 in R^n can be partitioned (the statement says covered; the literature usually says partitioned, and the sources do not say whether the two versions coincide for every set). The bullet asks for the value of f(n) as a function of n, in the sense of bounds. (b) Lower bounds on f(n): for each n, and asymptotically as n grows. (c) Upper bounds on f(n): for each n, and asymptotically as n grows. The statement names no dimension, no constant and no growth rate, and does not state the conjecture f(n) = n+1 in words; that conjecture is what the bullet's title points at, and counterexamples in a dimension n bear on it through the lower bound f(n) >= n+2. The bullet is open as a whole.

events.what_happened: Borsuk proved the planar case (n = 2) in 1932 (Verh. Internat. Math.-Kongr. Zurich 2, as cited by MathWorld) and posed the general question in 1933 (Fund. Math. 20). Known only from secondary citations; I did not open the 1932 or 1933 papers.
events.delivers: For n = 2 every bounded planar set of diameter 1 splits into 3 pieces of smaller diameter, so f(2) = 3. Positive result, dimension 2 only.
events.remains: All n >= 3 for the general problem.

checked_by.qualification: Refereed conference proceedings of the period

events.directly_checkable: The planar case is elementary and can be checked by hand; I did not check it.
events.direction: Supports the conjecture in the plane (3 = n+1 pieces suffice).

events.what_happened: Positive result for n = 3, credited on Wikipedia to Perkal (1947) and Eggleston (1955). Secondary citation only; the primary papers were not opened.
events.delivers: For n = 3 every bounded set of diameter 1 splits into 4 pieces of smaller diameter, so f(3) = 4. Dimension 3 only.
events.direction: Supports the conjecture in dimension 3.

events.what_happened: Positive results for restricted classes of sets, credited on Wikipedia to Hadwiger (1946, smooth convex bodies), Riesling (1971, centrally symmetric sets) and Dekster (1995, bodies of revolution). Secondary citation only.
events.delivers: The conjecture (f(n) = n+1) holds in every dimension for the named classes, and only for them. Restricted classes; the general statement is not settled by these.
events.remains: All sets not in the named classes.
events.direction: Supports the conjecture on the named classes.

events.what_happened: Lassak (Bull. Acad. Polon. Sci. Ser. Math. 30 (1982) 449-451, as cited in a bibliography quoted in search results) gives the elementary upper bound f(n) <= 2^(n-1)+1 for n >= 4, giving f(4) <= 9. This was the best known bound for n = 4 until May 2026. Secondary citation only; the 1982 paper was not opened.
events.delivers: Upper bound f(n) <= 2^(n-1)+1 for all n >= 4, so f(4) <= 9 and f(9) <= 257. Covers every dimension, not a restricted class.
events.remains: The asymptotic question (Schramm's bound below is much smaller for large n).
events.direction: Upper bound; no bearing on whether the conjecture holds.

events.what_happened: Schramm proves an asymptotic upper bound f(n) <= (sqrt(3/2)+o(1))^n by bounding the illumination number of constant-width bodies. Bourgain and Lindenstrauss (1989 or 1991, the sources differ) gave an independent covering argument. Secondary citation only (Wikipedia; the Bikeev-Raigorodskii 2025 introduction); the primary papers were not opened. One source dates Schramm's result to 1987.
events.delivers: Asymptotic upper bound f(n) <= (sqrt(3/2)+eps)^n for large n. Covers all n asymptotically.
events.remains: Whether the base sqrt(3/2) can be lowered (a survey, as reported in a search summary, lists this as open). Whether f(n) is exponential in n or in sqrt(n) is open between the bounds.
events.doubts: The year is given as 1987 by one source (a Prymak talk abstract) and 1988 by most; Bourgain-Lindenstrauss is dated 1989 or 1991.
events.direction: Upper bound; supports the conjecture only in the trivial sense that it is not contradicted.

events.what_happened: Raigorodskii (1999, On a bound in Borsuk's problem) improves the Kahn-Kalai lower bound to (1.2255...)^sqrt(n). The base is (2/sqrt(3))^sqrt(2), as written in the Bikeev-Raigorodskii 2025 introduction. Secondary citations only (a Prymak slide deck and the 2025 arXiv paper); the 1999 note was not opened.
events.delivers: Asymptotic lower bound f(n) >= (1.2255...+o(1))^sqrt(n) for large n.
events.remains: A lower bound exponential in n rather than in sqrt(n); the order of growth is open between sqrt(n) and n in the exponent.
events.direction: Lower bound; cuts against an f(n) that stays linear in n but does not bear on the conjecture at any fixed dimension.

events.what_happened: Kahn and Kalai (arXiv math/9307229, 1 July 1993; Bull. AMS 29 (1993) 60-62) prove f(d) >= (1.2)^sqrt(d) for large d, which disproves Borsuk's conjecture in high dimensions. Their concluding remarks state the construction works for d = 1325 and for every d > 2014 (as reported by secondary summaries; I did not see those remarks in the abstract). Weissbach (2000) remarked that the 1325 claim does not hold as stated; Jenrich's 2018 arXiv note, as reported in a search summary and not opened, says a missed halving can be recovered, giving 1325 to 1560.
events.revisions: Single arXiv version. Jenrich 2018 arXiv note on the 1325 claim (reported in a search summary, not opened). Journal version BAMS 29 (1993) 60-62.
events.delivers: Counterexamples to Borsuk's conjecture in all sufficiently large dimensions, with the lower bound f(d) >= (1.2)^sqrt(d) for large d (abstract, opened). The specific dimension threshold (1325, or 2014) is disputed as above.
events.remains: The exact threshold dimension; any bound below exponential in sqrt(d) (Raigorodskii 1999 improved the base).

checked_by.who: Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society

events.doubts: The 1325 dimension was disputed by Weissbach (2000) and, per a 2018 note reported in search results, repaired by Kretschmer's observation. I did not check either.
events.direction: Against Borsuk's conjecture in high dimensions.
events.object: Finite point sets with 0/1 coordinates, per a search snippet (not the body of the paper, which I did not read); the abstract itself does not describe the construction.

events.what_happened: Nilli (1994, On Borsuk's problem, Jerusalem Combinatorics '93, pp. 209-210) gives a counterexample in dimension 946. Secondary citations only (MathWorld references; Hinrichs 2002 summary; the Tao ledger table); the Nilli note was not opened.
events.delivers: Counterexample in dimension 946 (lower bound f(946) >= 948).
events.remains: Dimensions 65 to 945 among others, superseded later.
events.direction: Against the conjecture at n = 946.

events.remains: Dimensions 65 to 559 among others, superseded later.

events.what_happened: Hinrichs (2002, Discrete Mathematics note, generalising Kahn-Kalai via spherical codes and the Leech lattice) gives a set in R^323 that cannot be split into 561 pieces of smaller diameter. Secondary citation only (Hinrichs's note and the Tao ledger; not opened).
events.delivers: Counterexample in dimension 323.
events.remains: Dimensions 65 to 322 among others, superseded later.

Secondary citation only (Wikipedia and a discrete mathematics survey); the paper itself was not opened.

events.remains: Dimensions 4 to 297 (among others).
events.direction: Against the conjecture for n >= 298.

events.what_happened: Langi (arXiv 1007.2518, 'On the Borsuk number of four-dimensional sets', v1 15 Jul 2010) claims b(4) <= 8, improving Lassak's 9. The author withdrew the paper in v2 (11 Aug 2010) because of 'a crucial computational error in the proof of the lemma'.
events.revisions: v1 15 Jul 2010 (claim b(4) <= 8); v2 11 Aug 2010 (withdrawn, no content).
events.delivers: As claimed, b(4) <= 8. Withdrawn, so it establishes nothing as a current claim.
events.remains: b(4) <= 9 (Lassak) until the 2026 Tolmachev-Voronov result, and nothing else.
events.doubts: Withdrawn by the author for a computational error in a lemma. The lemma and the error are not described on the arXiv page I opened.

withdrawn.what: Withdrawn by the author: 'due to a crucial computational error in the proof of the lemma'

events.direction: Would have been an upper bound at n = 4; withdrawn.

events.what_happened: Bondarenko (arXiv 1305.2584, 12 May 2013, 'On Borsuk's conjecture for two-distance sets') gives a two-distance set of 416 points on the unit sphere in R^65 that cannot be partitioned into 83 pieces of smaller diameter (so at least 84). It answers Larman's question. The construction comes from the Euclidean representation of the G2(4) strongly regular graph. Published in Discrete Comput. Geom. 51 (2014) 509-515 (per MathWorld's references; not opened).
events.revisions: v1 12 May 2013; v2 19 May 2013; v3 29 Aug 2013 (current).
events.delivers: Counterexample in R^65: f(65) >= 84 (two-distance set). Wikipedia says the conjecture fails for all n >= 65 on this basis (secondary).
events.remains: Dimensions 4 to 64.
events.directly_checkable: The 416-point set is explicit (G2(4) representation); the 83-part bound is a computation I did not run.
events.direction: Against the conjecture at n = 65.
events.object: A two-distance set of 416 points on the unit sphere of R^65, from the G2(4) strongly regular graph (parameters 416,100,36,20), which cannot be partitioned into 83 pieces of smaller diameter.

events.what_happened: Jenrich (arXiv 1308.0206, 1 Aug 2013, 'A 64-dimensional two-distance counterexample to Borsuk's conjecture') gives a 64-dimensional subset of Bondarenko's 416-point set, with 352 points, that needs at least 71 pieces (Bondarenko's count for this subset is 72, per the abstract as summarised). The proof is computer-assisted by a small program (G24CHK). The journal version with Brouwer (Electronic J. Combin. 21(4) P4.29, published 2014 per search metadata) follows the same idea without the heavy computation; the journal page was not reachable.
events.revisions: v1 1 Aug 2013; v2 5 Aug 2013 (srg definition corrected); v3 11 Aug 2013; v4 19 Aug 2013; v5 25 Aug 2013; v6 20 Aug 2014.
events.delivers: Counterexample in R^64: f(64) >= 71 (two-distance set; computer-assisted).
events.remains: Dimensions 4 to 63.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the Jenrich-Brouwer version (21(4) P4.29, 2014) per search metadata

events.directly_checkable: The 352-point set is explicit as a subset of Bondarenko's set; the program G24CHK is included with the paper. I did not run it.
events.doubts: The argument depends on a computer program; I did not inspect it. The arXiv abstract notes the program runs in about one second on a 1 GHz processor.
events.direction: Against the conjecture at n = 64.
events.object: A 64-dimensional subset of Bondarenko's 416-point two-distance set, with 352 points, that cannot be partitioned into fewer than 71 pieces of smaller diameter.

events.what_happened: Arman, Bondarenko and Prymak (arXiv 2304.10418, 20 Apr 2023, v3 26 Jun 2024, 'Convex bodies of constant width with exponential illumination number') show that constant-width convex bodies in R^n have illumination number at least (cos(pi/14)+o(1))^(-n), answering a question of G. Kalai, and that some finite sets of diameter 1 cannot be covered by (2/sqrt(3)+o(1))^n balls of diameter 1.
events.delivers: Bounds on illumination numbers of constant-width bodies, and on covers by balls of diameter 1. These are different quantities from f(n): covers by balls of diameter 1 are not covers by pieces of strictly smaller diameter, and the illumination quantity concerns a route to upper bounds. I could not see a direct lower bound on f(n) from it.
events.remains: f(n) itself is unchanged by this paper.
events.direction: Neutral for the bullet's bounds; it is a neighbouring quantity (illumination and balls of diameter 1), not a counterexample to the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Jenrich (arXiv 2305.06283, 'Sub-25-dimensional counterexamples to Borsuk's conjecture in the Leech lattice?', first version 10 May 2023) builds sets from the 196,560 minimal vectors of the Leech lattice (diameter sqrt(96)) and from laminated sublattices. He reports having checked that divisions into at most n+1 parts exist for all n <= 21. For n = 22, 23 and 24 the smallest part-counts he found were 25, 29 and 34, which exceed n+1, and he describes a potential counterexample for n = 24. The paper asks a question in its title and claims no counterexample.
events.revisions: v2 29 Jun 2023 (n = 22 progress; correction); v3 2 Aug 2023 (six values of n); v4 7 Aug 2023 (potential counterexample file); v5 8 Apr 2024 (n = 14 and 20 progress); v6 13 Mar 2025 (n = 16, 19, 24 progress; effort description corrected).
events.delivers: For the specific Leech-lattice-derived sets: computational evidence that n+1 pieces suffice for n <= 21, and that the part-counts found for n = 22, 23, 24 exceed n+1. These part-counts are upper bounds on what was found, not lower bounds on what is needed. Establishes no counterexample in any dimension below 25.
events.remains: Whether these sets are counterexamples for n = 22 to 24 (requires a lower bound on the pieces needed); the bullet's bounds generally.
events.time_since_posted: about 3 years 5 months (first version to 11 Oct 2026); no public engagement found
events.directly_checkable: The sets are explicit (minimal Leech-lattice vectors) and a data file for n = 24 is included per the abstract; I did not run any of it.
events.doubts: The n = 22 to 24 part-counts are heuristic search results. The author does not claim a lower bound.
events.direction: Mixed: supports the conjecture for these sets in n <= 21; leaves n = 22 to 24 open with a potential counterexample at n = 24.
events.object: Sets built from the 196,560 minimal vectors of the Leech lattice (diameter sqrt(96)) and from laminated sublattices for smaller n. For n = 24 a data file encodes a set the author could not divide into fewer than 29 pieces (as stated in the abstract). Explicit, not constructed by proof.

events.what_happened: Tolmachev, Protasov and Voronov (arXiv 2210.12394, 22 Oct 2022; Discrete Applied Math. 320 (2022) 270-281) give an algorithm for sub-optimal partitions of planar sets into k pieces of smaller diameter, improving some estimates for 10 <= k <= 17, and show every unit-diameter set in R^3 splits into four subsets of diameter at most 0.966 (per the abstract, read through the fetch summary).
events.revisions: v1 only per arXiv page (journal reference DAM 320 (2022) 270-281).
events.delivers: Upper bounds on a diameter-constant variant in dimensions 2 and 3 (partitions of unit-diameter sets into k pieces of smaller diameter). Does not change f(2) = 3 or f(3) = 4, and does not change the general bounds.
events.remains: The general question.
events.doubts: A personal GitHub repository (vsvor/Borsuk-problem, see below) states that the authors' 3D numerical results contain errors and gives a corrected value of about 0.965399 (not verified by me).
events.direction: Variant upper bounds in dimensions 2 and 3; no direct bearing on the conjecture's status.

events.what_happened: Batmanov and Voronov (arXiv 2504.01233, 1 Apr 2025, 'The Borsuk Problem for Subsets of the Vertices of the 10-Dimensional Boolean Cube') show that every subset of the 10-cube can be partitioned into n+1 = 11 pieces of smaller diameter, extending earlier results for n <= 9 (Ziegler 2001; Goldstein 2012). Computer-assisted, with heuristics and the SAT solver kissat.
events.revisions: v1 1 Apr 2025 only as far as I checked; later versions not checked.
events.delivers: Discrete variant: subsets of the vertices of the 10-cube are partitioned into 11 pieces. Restricted to vertices of the cube, not to continuous sets in R^10.
events.remains: Continuous sets in every dimension; the bullet's bounds generally.
events.directly_checkable: Computer search (SAT); not checked by me.
events.direction: Supports the conjecture in a discrete analogue at n = 10.

events.what_happened: Ahmed (Chebyshevskii Sbornik, 2025, received December 2024, per a search snippet) shows that Bondarenko's 416-point two-distance construction also works in every l_p space. The search snippet says dimension 64; Bondarenko's paper gives R^65, so the snippet is inconsistent with the source. The journal page was not reachable.
events.delivers: Counterexamples of the Bondarenko type in l_p normed spaces. Different metric from the problem's Euclidean setting, so a different question.
events.remains: The Euclidean problem, unchanged.
events.doubts: Known only from a search snippet; the paper itself was not opened, and the dimension in the snippet conflicts with Bondarenko's.
events.direction: Counterexamples in a different metric, so no bearing on the Euclidean conjecture.

events.what_happened: Bikeev and Raigorodskii (arXiv 2508.14578, 20 Aug 2025, 'On upper bounds on the number of parts in the problem of partitioning sets into parts of smaller diameter') prove an upper bound for chi(n,b), the variant in which parts must have diameter strictly less than b in (0,1]; chi(n,1) = f(n). Theorem 1: chi(n,b) <= (sqrt(1/b^2+1/2)+o(1))^n. At b = 1 this gives (sqrt(3/2)+o(1))^n, which is Schramm's bound, so the result does not move f(n).
events.revisions: One version (v1, 20 Aug 2025) per the arXiv page.
events.delivers: A new upper bound for the variant chi(n,b) with b < 1, asymptotically in n. At b = 1 it equals the Schramm bound, so for f(n) it reproduces an existing result rather than improving it.
events.remains: f(n) for all n (no new bound at b = 1 in the sections read).
events.doubts: I read the abstract and introduction only (HTML). The paper's body was not read in full, so I cannot rule out a b = 1 result later in the text; the abstract says it finds a new upper bound for chi(n,b).
events.direction: Variant upper bound; at b = 1 the same as Schramm's, so it does not move the bullet.

events.what_happened: Averkov, Brose, De Loera, Lopez-Campos and Torres (arXiv 2508.20009, 27 Aug 2025, 'On Lattice Diameter Segments: Algorithms and Structure'; v2 3 Oct 2026) study the lattice diameter of sets and prove a Borsuk-type theorem: how many parts a set of lattice points must be split into so that each part has strictly smaller lattice diameter.
events.delivers: A Borsuk-type theorem for a discrete notion (lattice diameter, lattice points). Discrete analogue, not Euclidean sets of diameter 1.
events.remains: The continuous problem.
events.direction: Discrete analogue; no bearing on the continuous bound.

events.what_happened: Musin (arXiv 2511.03668, 5 Nov 2025, v2 15 Nov 2025, 'Borsuk's conjecture for two-distance sets and its equivalent formulation for graphs') reformulates the two-distance-set analogue of the conjecture in terms of graphs, and states that the two-distance version remains open for dimensions 4 to 63. Per a search summary, he reports no two-distance counterexample for d = 4, confirmed by Szollosi's enumeration; I did not verify that part from the abstract.
events.delivers: A reformulation for two-distance sets (graphs). It is an analogue of the conjecture, not the Euclidean problem, and it states the two-distance version as open in dimensions 4 to 63.
events.remains: The Euclidean conjecture; the two-distance analogue in every dimension.
events.direction: Analogue; no bearing on the Euclidean bounds. States the two-distance version open for 4 to 63.

events.what_happened: Caceres, Garijo, Marquez and Silveira (arXiv 2604.11651, 13 Apr 2026, 'The Borsuk number of a graph') define a graph analogue of the Borsuk problem (partition by vertices or by continuous edges) and give complexity results, exact computations and upper bounds on graph parameters.
events.revisions: v1 13 Apr 2026; later versions not checked.
events.delivers: Graph analogue; results on graph parameters, not on f(n).
events.remains: The Euclidean problem.
events.direction: Analogue; no bearing on the Euclidean bounds.

events.what_happened: Tolmachev and Voronov (arXiv 2605.19068, 18 May 2026, 'Reducing the upper bound for the Borsuk number in R^4 to 8') construct partitions of several variants of the truncated Lassak cover into 8 parts of diameter less than 1, and state Theorem 2: any set of unit diameter in R^4 can be partitioned into 8 parts of diameter less than 0.9999. The method is a computer search (scipy, qhull, PyTorch with Adam, Nelder-Mead, a black-box optimiser), taking about 10 CPU days on a 32-core EPYC 7532. The paper says exact diameter computation is technically complicated and does not state that exact arithmetic was used. The conclusion says the method is unlikely to prove the conjecture in dimension 4.
events.revisions: v1 18 May 2026 only (per arXiv page).
events.delivers: Upper bound b(4) <= 8 (from 9). Settles no lower bound and not the conjecture in dimension 4; it is a single-dimension upper bound.
events.remains: f(4) between 5 and 8 (the conjecture would give 5); all other dimensions.
events.directly_checkable: The partitions are numerical; a reader can check the claimed diameters by computation. The paper's own text says exact diameter computation is technically complicated, so the 0.9999 margin rests on approximate diameter estimates (quoted from the paper's method section).
events.doubts: Numerical method with approximate diameter estimates (quoted above). The introduction calls 9 the best known bound and does not mention Langi's 2010 withdrawn claim of 8 (the fetched text does not mention Langi at all). No review found.
events.direction: Moves an upper bound at n = 4 down by one; cuts toward the conjecture only in the trivial sense that it does not contradict it.
events.object: Explicit partitions of several variants of the truncated Lassak cover into 8 parts of diameter less than 1, found numerically; the paper gives no closed-form partition.

ai.disclosed_cost: About 10 CPU days on a workstation with an EPYC 7532 CPU (32 cores), per the paper.

events.what_happened: Grinsztajn's public GitHub repository maaxgrin/borsuk-63-counterexample (created 26 May 2026 20:30:54 UTC; first commit 'Add Borsuk 63 verification note' at 20:31:06 UTC; 16 commits by the account maaxgrin up to 27 May 2026 09:49 UTC) gives a proof note (PDF, not readable by me) and an exact verification script claiming a 63-dimensional counterexample to Borsuk's conjecture (d_B <= 63). The README says the construction is the G2(4) model over F16 with a partition of the 416-vertex strongly regular graph into 96 and 320 vertices, and that the previous best was d_B <= 64 (Jenrich-Brouwer). The README says: 'The construction and proof were obtained with assistance from GPT-5.5 Pro.' Wikipedia (snapshot 8 Oct 2026) and MathWorld credit the result to Max Grinsztajn with GPT-5.5 Pro and describe a 321-point configuration with at least 65 pieces. The README text I read does not state the 321-point set. The account is identified with the Wikipedia name by me, not by the repository.
events.revisions: 16 commits 26 to 27 May 2026. Commits include 'Disclose GPT assistance' (26 May 22:02 UTC), 'Add proof PDF and clarify README' (27 May 00:32 UTC) and 'Update proof PDF' (27 May 08:40 UTC). The PDF's versions were not read.
events.delivers: As the README states it: Borsuk's conjecture fails in dimension 63 (d_B <= 63), by a G2(4)-based construction with a partition into 96 and 320 vertices, and exact finite-field verification. The 321-point set, and the claim b(63) >= 65, are reported by Wikipedia, MathWorld and the Ji preprint, and I could not confirm them in the README text.
events.remains: All other dimensions; the conjecture in dimensions 4 to 62 is untouched.

checked_by.what_they_did: Approved the formal statement PR that includes the 63 counterexample

machine_checked.system: Python exact verification (verify_borsuk63.py, finite field F16 reconstruction) with GitHub Actions CI; optional Sage check on DIMACS certificates

events.directly_checkable: verify_borsuk63.py reconstructs the G2(4) model over F16 and checks the parameters, the partition, the component structure and the clique obstructions, per the README. I did not run it.
events.doubts: (1) The README text I read gives a 416-vertex graph with a 96 + 320 partition and does not state a 321-point set, while Wikipedia, MathWorld and the Ji preprint describe a 321-point set. (2) Wikipedia calls the configuration a three-distance configuration; the README and the Ji preprint describe a two-distance embedding of the G2(4) graph, and ThePromptIndex says the same. events.direction: Cuts against Borsuk's conjecture in dimension 63 (counterexample, as the README states it).
events.object: Per the README: a G2(4) strongly regular graph (416 vertices, parameters 416,100,36,20) over F16, partitioned into a set of 96 and a set of 320, with a finite-field verification. Per Wikipedia and MathWorld: a 321-point set in R^63 with clique number 5 (so any smaller-diameter subset has at most five points, forcing at least 65 pieces). Explicit construction, checked by exact computation rather than a proof by hand. The 321-point set itself is not stated in the README text I read.

events.what_happened: Yibo Ji (arXiv 2608.12561, v1 12 Aug 2026, 'An AI Generated Counterexample to Borsuk Problem in Dimension 63', math.MG) claims a 321-point set in R^63 that cannot be partitioned into 64 subsets of smaller diameter, so b(63) >= 65, built from the G2(4) Euclidean representation and the Jenrich-Brouwer 320-point core by adding one projected and rescaled point. The abstract says the example and proof were 'generated entirely by ChatGPT using GPT-5.6 Sol'. The author says they verified the result personally, takes responsibility for it, claims no credit for the construction's originality, and does not wish to be regarded as an author. The v1 appendix contains a verification program (verify_borsuk_63.py) that reconstructs the graph from the Hermitian unital in PG(2,16); I did not run it. v2 (14 Aug 2026) is withdrawn with the comment 'Just found out that this counterexample had already been posted elsewhere', linking external repositories and a project page, and the notice 'This paper has been withdrawn by Yibo Ji'. No reason beyond that is given.

events.what_happened: One manuscript, 'A nine-dimensional counterexample to Borsuk's covering assertion' (credited to OpenAI, dated 23 September 2026), claims that X = {uuᵀ : u ∈ ℝ⁴, |u| = 1}, the set of rank-one orthogonal projectors on ℝ⁴ inside the nine-dimensional trace-one affine space of real symmetric 4×4 matrices with the Frobenius metric, has diameter √2 and cannot be covered by ten subsets of diameter strictly less than √2. Its main theorem states this and writes it as b(X) > 10, where b(Y) is the least number of pieces of strictly smaller diameter needed to cover Y. The same manuscript's corollary extends this to every dimension d ≥ 9: for each such d there is a compact subset of ℝᵈ of diameter √2 that cannot be covered by d+1 subsets of strictly smaller diameter. It is built from a translate of X in ℝ⁹ together with s = d−9 further points, which lie at mutual distance √2 from each other and from every point of the translate (vectors with Gram matrix I_s + (1/4)·11ᵀ). The proof of the main theorem is topological and combinatorial. A cover by pieces of diameter below √2 yields a smooth partition of unity on ℝP³ whose positive supports are disjoint for orthogonal lines. Extending the resulting map to symmetric matrices gives an odd map from the 9-sphere to the 9-sphere. Its mod-two degree forces every maximal support to have four labels, with their sum a simplicial cycle. Degree and double-cover counts then force a six-label triangle system on the complement of each tetrahedral support, and a combinatorial analysis of these systems across adjacent tetrahedra gives a contradiction, so no admissible map ℝP³ → Δ⁹ exists.
events.delivers: For the bullet's lower-bound part: the manuscript exhibits a compact set in ℝ⁹ of diameter √2 that cannot be covered by ten pieces of strictly smaller diameter, so the minimum number of pieces for that set is at least 11, i.e. f(9) ≥ 11. By the corollary, for every d ≥ 9 some compact set in ℝᵈ needs at least d+2 pieces, giving f(d) ≥ d+2 for all d ≥ 9. This disproves the conjecture that d+1 pieces always suffice in each of those dimensions. Restrictions: the bounds are lower bounds only, and they apply to d ≥ 9. The manuscript says nothing about dimensions 8 and below and does not claim the conjecture fails there. The examples have diameter √2 rather than 1; the piece count is unchanged by scaling. The manuscript states the covering form, which matches the list's wording. It also remarks that covers and partitions give the same count, because overlaps can be removed without increasing diameters. That remark bears on the cover-versus-partition question the frozen statement leaves open. The manuscript does not claim to settle the problem. It says the theorem 'does not determine the smallest dimension in which it fails or the exact value of b(X)'.
events.remains: If the claim is correct, still open: the exact value of f(n) in every dimension, and the exact value of b(X) (only b(X) > 10 is proved). Also open: the smallest dimension in which the covering assertion fails, including whether it fails in any dimension from 2 to 8, which the manuscript does not address. Every upper bound on f(n) is open; the manuscript gives none. The growth of f(n) as n increases is open too: the manuscript's only new bound is the linear lower bound n+2.

machine_checked.scope: Borsuk's conjecture predicts that every bounded subset of $\mathbb R^d$ can be covered by $d+1$ sets of strictly smaller diameter. The formalized counterexample is the compact set of rank-one orthogonal projectors onto lines in $\mathbb R^4$, with the Frobenius metric. It lies in the nine-dimensional affine space of trace-one symmetric matrices, has diameter $\sqrt2$, and cannot be covered by ten arbitrary sets of smaller diameter.

events.doubts: (1) The non-coverability proof is a long hand argument spanning the geometry, topology, six-label and ten-label sections. The text reports no computer check. (2) Several combinatorial steps are compressed into a sentence and are not flagged as sketched: the 'realizes every possible choice of omissions' step in the partner-block lemma; the claim in the two-tetrahedra lemma that the transported systems 'agree everywhere' from agreement on five labels; and, in the six-label lemma, the statement that a perpendicular line 'could use none of the six labels', where the contradiction also uses that a line's coordinates sum to one, which the text leaves implicit. (3) The claim that the result improves the dimension bound from 63 rests on a cited public note (Grinsztajn 2026), which the manuscript neither proves nor uses in its argument.
events.direction: disproves the conjecture f(n) = n+1 for every n ≥ 9 (lower bound f(n) ≥ n+2)
events.object: The set X = {uuᵀ : u ∈ ℝ⁴ unit}, the image of ℝP³ under u ↦ uuᵀ, is explicit. The manuscript gives an explicit isometry from its trace-one matrix space to ℝ⁹ in a remark on Euclidean coordinates. Its non-coverability is proved by a contradiction argument, not by an explicit certificate. For d ≥ 10 the added points are given by the explicit Gram matrix I_s + (1/4)·11ᵀ, which determines them up to an orthogonal change of basis.

disputes.summary: The dimension-63 counterexample is credited to Grinsztajn (repository from 26 May 2026, README: 'assistance from GPT-5.5 Pro'; Wikipedia and MathWorld) and to Ji (arXiv v1 12 Aug 2026, 'generated entirely by ChatGPT using GPT-5.6 Sol'; withdrawn 14 Aug 2026 with the comment that it 'had already been posted elsewhere'). A Lean PR commit message credits 'Konz and Ji' with independent finds; I found no source for Konz. Ji's appendix independently reconstructs the same F16 model. I did not resolve whether these are one result or two.

The same 63-dimensional object is attributed to GPT-5.5 Pro (Grinsztajn's README and Wikipedia; Wikipedia's AI-discoveries list says 'prompted GPT-5.5 Pro to discover') and to ChatGPT using GPT-5.6 Sol (Ji's abstract). The wording of the AI role also differs: 'obtained with assistance from' (README) versus 'generated entirely by' (Ji).

Construction type for the 63-dimensional object: Wikipedia calls it 'a 321-point three-distance configuration'; the README, Ji's preprint and ThePromptIndex describe a two-distance embedding of the G2(4) strongly regular graph (416,100,36,20). The README text I read does not state the 321-point set at all.

Dimension 9. OpenAI's repository and DeepMind's formal-conjectures PR #6898 record Borsuk's conjecture as refuted at n = 9. Wikipedia's Borsuk article (snapshot 8 Oct 2026) and the Tao ledger row for constant 28 (no date shown) still give 63 as the smallest known failing dimension. The two records conflict until the nine-dimensional claim is checked or a publication or correction appears.

Covering versus partition. The bullet and the nine-dimensional claim speak of covering by ten sets of smaller diameter; the classical Borsuk problem is stated for partitions. The sources do not say whether the two versions give the same f(n) for these sets, and I did not settle it.

Statement fidelity of the Lean theorem for the nine-dimensional claim. The linked theorem was first a matrix-space statement and was changed to EuclideanSpace R (Fin 9). The PR author states that the remaining gap is diam versus ediam and intersecting the cover with the set.

Dimension 4. Langi (arXiv 1007.2518, 2010) claimed b(4) <= 8 and withdrew it in August 2010 for a computational error in a lemma. Tolmachev and Voronov (arXiv 2605.19068, May 2026) claim b(4) <= 8, and their introduction calls 9 the best known bound and does not mention Langi's claim. The Lean PR cites their result without comment on priority.

A personal repository (vsvor/Borsuk-problem) says the Tolmachev-Protasov-Voronov 2022 numerics for the 3D covering constant contain errors, and gives a corrected value of about 0.965399 (variant; not checked by me). The repository is not established as having any connection to the paper's authors beyond shared surnames.

OpenAI's manuscript count: 722 at release (secondary coverage, Kalai), 719 in the repository's current README, and 377 in one report. Also one tracker reports 3 withdrawn and 14 revised results on 7 Oct 2026. I did not identify any of these with the Borsuk item.

The 1325 dimension in the Kahn-Kalai remarks. Weissbach (2000) observed it does not hold as stated; per a 2018 note by Jenrich (reported in search results, not opened), a fix gives counterexamples for dimensions 1325 to 1560. The sources differ on whether the fix is accepted.
The Wikipedia AI-discoveries list spells the name 'Grinzstajn' in its body and 'Grinsztajn' in its references. The record uses 'Grinsztajn' as the repository and MathWorld spell it.

summary: The bullet asks for upper and lower bounds on the least number of smaller-diameter pieces needed for bounded n-dimensional sets, and the general asymptotic bounds are unchanged in every source I read: Kahn-Kalai's lower bound (1.2)^sqrt(n) was improved by Raigorodskii (1999) to order 1.2255^sqrt(n), and Schramm gives an upper bound of order (sqrt(3/2))^n; the 2025 Bikeev-Raigorodskii paper reproduces Schramm at b = 1. The per-dimension record has moved in three ways since January 2024. (1) A 63-dimensional counterexample: Grinsztajn's public repository (first commit 26 May 2026) claims one with 'assistance from GPT-5.5 Pro'; Ji's arXiv preprint (12 Aug 2026) claims the same dimension and point count, says it was 'generated entirely by ChatGPT using GPT-5.6 Sol', and was withdrawn two days later with a comment that the counterexample had already been posted elsewhere. The README I read does not state the 321-point set that Wikipedia, MathWorld and Ji describe, so I could not confirm the point count from the primary source I opened, and I did not resolve whether the two postings are one construction or two. (2) Dimension 4: Tolmachev and Voronov (18 May 2026) claim b(4) <= 8 by an approximate computer search, improving Lassak's 9; Langi's 2010 claim of 8 was withdrawn. (3) On 6 Oct 2026 OpenAI's openai/math release catalogued a nine-dimensional counterexample to the covering version, 'Borsuk's conjecture fails in dimension nine', with a Lean statement (EuclideanSpace R (Fin 9)) that DeepMind's formal-conjectures project linked and marked as refuted on 11 Oct 2026. The construction is explicit (rank-one projectors onto lines in R^4, Frobenius metric, diameter sqrt(2)); the diameter follows by hand; the impossibility of a ten-piece cover I could not check, because the preprint PDF and the Lean file were unreadable to me. No human expert account of this result was found, and Wikipedia and the Tao ledger still give 63. Read as a counterexample, it lowers the smallest known failing dimension from 63 to 9, but it moves the bullet's bounds only at n = 9. Close calls: whether the 63-dimensional result is one construction or two; whether the AI attribution for the nine-dimensional item (a repository-wide statement, not a Borsuk-specific sentence) is enough; and whether the covering version used in the release and the partition version in the literature agree for these sets. Discounted analogues and neighbours: Musin (two-distance sets; open for 4 to 63), Bikeev-Raigorodskii (variant chi(n,b)), Batmanov-Voronov (10-cube, discrete), Averkov et al. (lattice diameter), Caceres et al. (graph Borsuk number), Ahmed (l_p, known only from a snippet), vsvor (3D covering constant with a GPT-6 Astra claim), Arman-Bondarenko-Prymak (illumination and covers by balls of diameter 1), and Jenrich's Leech-lattice computations (no counterexample claimed in dimensions 22 to 24). The Lean formalisation PR #5265 (Sep 2026) states the 63 case and says it was 'assisted by Claude Code', which concerns formalisation and is not counted as AI involvement in the mathematics.
competing_reading: Read the nine-dimensional claim as a large move: a counterexample in dimension 9 would cut the smallest known failing dimension from 63 to 9, is linked into a second formal project, and is the single most important per-dimension event in the window. Read it as a small move: it is one dimension and a covering version; the only public support is OpenAI's own repository, a Lean statement whose faithfulness was contested in review and whose proof-level checks were partly not run (#print axioms and Comparator), and an unreviewed preprint I could not read; and the bullet asks for bounds for all n, which this claim does not change beyond f(9) >= 11. For the 63-dimensional result the competing reading is that Ji's preprint is an independent discovery: its appendix reconstructs the F16 model from scratch, and the Lean PR says Ji and Konz found it independently. The reading against that is that the withdrawal comment points to an earlier posting, and no source for Konz was found.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The openai/math preprint paper.pdf (full text and build) and the Lean module path for OAI.BorsukNine.euclidean_nine_counterexample, with #print axioms and a Comparator run on that theorem. (2) A public written check of the nine-dimensional argument by a named mathematician, or an arXiv or journal posting. (3) OpenAI's own statement (the primary announcement was unreachable to me) of which internal model produced item 156, and how. (4) Grinsztajn's proof note PDF (borsuk_63_counterexample.pdf) to see whether it states the 321-point set and whether it names Ji or Konz. (5) Konz's identity and any written work. (6) Ji's withdrawal reason, and the 'elsewhere' posting it refers to. (7) A statement on whether the covering and partition versions agree for these sets. (8) Updates to Wikipedia's Borsuk article and to the Tao ledger row for constant 28. (9) The Tolmachev-Voronov paper's full text, to confirm the method's exactness and whether it cites Langi's 2010 claim.

event.what_happened: Tolmachev and Voronov (arXiv 2605.19068, 18 May 2026, 'Reducing the upper bound for the Borsuk number in R^4 to 8') construct partitions of several variants of the truncated Lassak cover into 8 parts of diameter less than 1, and state Theorem 2: any set of unit diameter in R^4 can be partitioned into 8 parts of diameter less than 0.9999. The method is a computer search (scipy, qhull, PyTorch with Adam, Nelder-Mead, a black-box optimiser), taking about 10 CPU days on a 32-core EPYC 7532. The paper says exact diameter computation is technically complicated and does not state that exact arithmetic was used. The conclusion says the method is unlikely to prove the conjecture in dimension 4.
event.delivers: Upper bound b(4) <= 8 (from 9). Settles no lower bound and not the conjecture in dimension 4; it is a single-dimension upper bound.
event.remains: f(4) between 5 and 8 (the conjecture would give 5); all other dimensions.
event.directly_checkable: The partitions are numerical; a reader can check the claimed diameters by computation. The paper's own text says exact diameter computation is technically complicated, so the 0.9999 margin rests on approximate diameter estimates (quoted from the paper's method section).
event.doubts: Numerical method with approximate diameter estimates (quoted above). The introduction calls 9 the best known bound and does not mention Langi's 2010 withdrawn claim of 8 (the fetched text does not mention Langi at all). No review found.
event.direction: Moves an upper bound at n = 4 down by one; cuts toward the conjecture only in the trivial sense that it does not contradict it.
event.object: Explicit partitions of several variants of the truncated Lassak cover into 8 parts of diameter less than 1, found numerically; the paper gives no closed-form partition.

judgement.why: The statement asks for upper and lower bounds on f(n) in general. Its wording names no conjecture and no dimension, so a counterexample in one dimension, or even the claimed f(d) >= d+2 for every d >= 9, is a lower bound on f(n) and leaves the question open: scope bound. Per-dimension values in the plane and in R^3, and results for restricted classes, are cases. The three post-snapshot bound events that survive are Tolmachev-Voronov f(4) <= 8 (human, numerical, doubtful), Grinsztajn's 63 counterexample (an exact verification script on an explicit object, so checkable; GPT-5.5 Pro is credited with the construction and proof 'with assistance', so assisted rather than generated), and the OpenAI nine-dimensional result (unreviewed; generated, on the repository-wide statement). Ji's preprint is withdrawn, so I answered knocked_down even though the reason was duplication rather than an error. Musin, Bikeev-Raigorodskii, the lattice, graph, l_p, Boolean-cube and 3D covering-constant papers concern changed questions (variant). The Lean PRs are formalisation or linkage (none). acprk is numerical instances, and its AI assistants did nothing on this problem's mathematics that the record can identify. Counterexample objects are marked counterexample against the n+1 conjecture the bullet points to, but their direction is null because the scope is bound.

The OpenAI AI attribution rests on a repository-wide sentence, not one specific to Borsuk. The Lean statement had a reported diam/ediam gap, and the hand proof has compressed combinatorial steps; no named expert has checked it. Whether the 63 object is the 321-point set is unconfirmed in the README. Whether Grinsztajn's role should be 'generated' turns on the vague phrase 'with assistance'.
